title: Where not to camp or build a shelter
def: Choose a shelter site away from hazards overhead and underfoot: dead branches, rockfall, flood channels, game trails, and low cold pockets.
look: dead limbs or leaning trees overhead (widowmakers)
dry washes, gullies, and stream banks that can flood
loose rock above, ant nests, or a game trail through the spot
use: Look up before you look down. Pick a flat, well-drained spot on a bench or low slope, near building materials and water but 200 feet (60 m) from it, out of the wind. Put the latrine downhill and downstream.
not: Do not camp under dead trees or in a drainage, and do not camp right on the shore of a stream or lake.
call: If a storm is coming, move away from tall lone trees and low channels.

title: Debris hut (how to build)
also: hut made of leaves and sticks
def: A debris hut is a small, wedge-shaped shelter of a ridgepole, ribs, and a thick layer of dry leaves or other debris, built to trap body heat.
look: a long ridgepole on a stump, rock, or tripod
ribs steep enough to shed water
at least about 3 feet (1 m) of dry debris outside and 2 feet (60 cm) of bedding inside
use: Build it when you need a warm shelter and have time and a lot of dry debris. Make it just big enough for your body, and close the entrance with a pile of debris or your pack.
not: Do not build it in a drain or under dead trees. Do not burn a stove, charcoal, or a candle in a closed hut.
steps: Prop a long ridgepole on a stump or a tripod.
Lean ribs along both sides of the pole, close together.
Cover the ribs with a lattice of small sticks so insulation does not fall in.
Pile 3 feet of dry leaves, grass, or ferns on top and cover with branches against wind.
Stuff the inside with bedding, crawl in feet first, and close the entrance.
call: Leave a way for air to move; fuel-burning devices make carbon monoxide.

title: Lean-to with a fire reflector
def: A lean-to is a sloped roof with an open side, built against a crossbar between two trees or posts, often with a fire reflector wall opposite it.
look: a crossbar between two supports at about chest height
a roof sloping toward the wind with the open side away from it
a fire reflector wall of logs or rocks a few feet in front
use: Use it when you need a quick shelter in calm to moderate weather. Place the back to the wind, shingle the roof from the bottom up, and add a thick bed. Keep the fire a few steps out and low.
not: Do not put a fire too close to the roof, and do not use a lean-to in strong winds from the open side.
call: Check for dead limbs overhead and keep the fire small.

title: Rigging a tarp or poncho shelter
also: how to set up a tarp
def: A tarp shelter is a sheet of waterproof fabric pitched over a ridgeline and staked down; it is the fastest shelter to set up.
look: a taut ridgeline between two trees at waist height
tarp draped over it with edges staked low
one end lowered into the wind
use: Tie a ridgeline between two trees, drape the tarp over it, and stake the corners. Pitch the low end into the wind and keep the high end open for air. Put a ground sheet under you.
not: Do not pitch it flat where water pools, or too high where wind can get under.

title: Ground insulation: why the ground comes first
def: The ground pulls heat out of you faster than the air does, so insulation under you matters before the roof.
look: a 6 to 8 inch (15 to 20 cm) pressed layer of dry boughs, leaves, or grass
a pad or pack under your torso and hips
no direct contact with cold ground or snow
use: Build the bed first, then the shelter. Pile dry leaves, pine boughs (cut ends down), or grass, add a pad or pack, and refresh each night.
not: Do not lie on bare ground, rock, or snow.

title: What I can use for a shelter door
def: A shelter door is anything that closes the entrance against wind and cold, such as a pack, a debris pile, or a tarp.
look: a gap just big enough to crawl in
a door that can be closed from the inside
air flow through a small gap
use: Use your pack, a bundle of branches stuffed with leaves, a spare tarp, or a slab of snow. Close it from the inside after you crawl in, and leave a small gap for air.
not: Do not seal a shelter airtight when burning a candle or stove.

title: Stopping wind versus staying insulated
def: A windbreak stops moving air from stealing heat, while insulation traps still air around you; a good shelter does both.
look: windbreak: a wall, tarp, or log between you and the wind
insulation: dry layers, boughs, and a bed
moisture: wet insulation does not insulate
use: Block the wind first, then add insulation under and around you. Keep it dry and make the space small to hold heat.
not: Do not think a roof alone will keep you warm; the ground and wind steal the most heat.

title: Clothing as shelter: layering
def: Layering uses a wicking base, a warm insulating middle, and a windproof, waterproof outer layer that you adjust to stay dry and warm.
look: wool or synthetic base layers, not cotton
an insulating mid-layer like fleece or down
a shell for wind and rain, plus hat, gloves, and dry socks
use: Vent before you sweat, add layers when you stop, and swap wet layers for dry ones as soon as you can. Keep a spare dry layer in a waterproof bag.
not: Do not wear cotton in cold or wet weather; it holds water and chills you.

title: No fuel burning in a closed shelter
def: Burning charcoal, a stove, a lantern, or even a candle in a closed shelter can fill it with carbon monoxide, which has no smell and can kill in your sleep.
look: a closed tent, snow cave, car, or hut
headache and drowsiness
a flame that burns low or yellow from lack of air
use: Cook and heat outside or in a well-ventilated vestibule, and leave a vent open at all times. Use a battery lantern inside. Carry a battery CO alarm in a tent when you can.
not: Do not burn charcoal, a camp stove, or a heater in a tent, snow cave, or vehicle.
call: Get out into fresh air and call 911 for headache, dizziness, or confusion in a closed space.

title: Stuck in a car in a snowstorm
def: If stranded in a car in a snowstorm, staying with the vehicle is usually safest; keep the tailpipe clear and run the engine only a little.
look: blowing or falling snow with low visibility
the exhaust pipe at risk of blocking
engine running in an enclosed space
use: Call 911, tie a bright cloth to the antenna, and stay in the car. Run the engine about 10 minutes each hour with the tailpipe clear of snow and a window cracked. Keep moving your arms and legs and keep warm layers on.
not: Do not leave the car in a whiteout unless help is clearly in sight, and do not let the tailpipe get blocked.
call: Call 911; carbon monoxide can build up in a car with a blocked tailpipe.

title: Snow shelters: tree-pit and ventilation
def: A snow shelter uses snow's insulating quality, and it needs a vent hole and a roof about a foot thick to be safe.
look: a tree well with low branches overhead
a trench or cave with a roof at least 12 inches (30 cm) thick
a fist-sized vent hole in the roof
use: Dig a pit under an evergreen, roof it with branches and snow, line the floor with boughs, and cut a vent. Keep a tool inside and keep the entrance lower than the sleeping area.
not: Do not sweat while digging, and do not burn fuel inside. Keep the vent open.
call: Check the vent often; snow can block it.

title: Space blanket and bivy: what they will and won't do
def: A space blanket is a thin reflective sheet that holds in some body heat; a bivy is a waterproof shell for a sleeping bag.
look: a very light sheet that reflects heat back
a bivy keeps wind and rain off a bag
condensation builds inside if there is no vent
use: Wrap a space blanket around you under clothes or in a shelter, with a pad or dry layers under you. Use it as a roof or wind block too. Add insulation; it does not warm by itself.
not: Do not rely on it alone in cold or wet weather, and do not seal yourself in without a vent.

title: Tent site and storm pitching
also: set up a tent in the wind
def: For a storm pitch, set the tent low and tight with the narrow end into the wind, and guy out every line.
look: a flat, drained site away from dead trees
the door facing away from the wind
taut guy lines and deep stakes or rocks
use: Choose a protected spot, stake every corner and guy line, and stow the pack inside. Put rocks or logs on the stakes in soft ground. Avoid ridges and open meadows.
not: Do not camp under tall dead trees or in a dry wash during a storm.

title: Fire placement near a shelter
also: how close should a fire be
def: Place a fire off the opening of a shelter and far enough that sparks cannot reach the roof or bedding.
look: a fire 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) from a tarp or tent
a reflector wall behind the fire
no overhanging branches
use: Keep the fire small and downwind of the shelter, away from the door and dry fabric. Use a ring of rocks or a pit. Put it out before you sleep.
not: Do not build a fire inside a tent or under the roof of a tarp.

title: Shelter for rain, wind, snow, and bugs
def: Different weather needs a different shelter: a steep tarp for rain, a low wedge for wind, a snow shelter for deep snow, and netting for insects.
look: rain: steep pitch and a drip line
wind: low and streamlined, back to the wind
snow: dug into the snowpack with a vent
insects: a fine mesh net or smoke
use: Pick the shelter that fits what the weather is doing, and use netting or a head net when insects are bad.
not: Do not rely on smoke to keep bugs away in a closed shelter.

title: Group versus solo shelter
def: A group shelter shares body heat and takes less material per person; a solo shelter must be smaller and better insulated.
look: two people sharing a bag or insulation hold heat better
a smaller space is warmer
shared watch duties
use: Share a larger shelter where possible, huddle with insulation under all, and take turns keeping the vent and fire.
not: Do not crowd so tightly that air cannot move.

title: How much insulation is enough?
also: how thick should the leaves be
def: In plain terms, thicker is warmer: about 3 feet of dry debris on a hut and 6 to 8 inches under you, with a small vent.
look: 3 feet (1 m) of debris on a hut
6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) under you
dry, fluffy material, not wet or packed
use: Add more until you can no longer feel the cold coming through, and keep it dry. Leave a vent.
not: Do not use wet leaves or packed snow alone as a bed.
